paragraphs.opening: In retrieval-augmented generation, retaining a source does not guarantee delivery of its required factual support.
Context construction is a data-processing pipeline that determines which retrieved evidence reaches a RAG generator.
A page can remain in the context even when a required assertion from that page has been removed or truncated.
This distinction raises a measurement question that source-level outcomes alone cannot answer.
We investigate this question using paired source groupings and interval-level traces of delivered support.
The study contributes a measured evaluation blind spot, a stage-level explanation, and an account of the finding's practical limits.
We model evidence delivery as retrieval followed by source capping, re-ranking, and budgeted packing.
Candidate membership, scoring visibility, and delivered text are three distinct views of the same evidence.
Designated-page retention and complete fact coverage test different properties of the final context.
The two endpoints are not interchangeable, and complete support can coexist with conflicting evidence.
We reconstruct support from original text intervals and keep source policy, ranking, and answer grounding as separate endpoints.
The benchmark supplies known facts and support spans in independently generated fictional collections.
Paired variants alter URL grouping while preserving the question and ordered document texts.
The designed workload varies support structure, document rendering, and the number of required facts.
The configuration matrix varies retrieval, cap placement, scoring views, and packing under explicitly matched conditions.
The uncapped comparison diagnoses the measurement gap, whereas the cap-order comparisons test operator placement.
Structural controls test whether the measurement and pipeline operations preserve support in cases where they should.
Statistical inference treats worlds, rather than their paired variants, as independent units.
Answer generation, request timing, and complementary workloads use separate samples and evaluation protocols.
We first establish the measurement gap, then trace evidence loss across pipeline stages and workload conditions before assessing answers and request cost.
At 2048 tokens, post-capping preserves every designated-page retention outcome while reducing complete fact coverage.
Agreement in page retention conceals task-level losses and gains in complete support.
The comparison reveals a limitation of source-level evaluation, not an advantage of imposing a source cap.
With identical retrieved candidates, cap placement changes the complete support available before packing.
The 512-token budget removes the observed cap-order difference at the delivery boundary.
A larger budget exposes a small post-cap advantage in the prespecified placement comparison.
The structural controls distinguish deletion of supporting content from changes in its order.
A surviving chunk can still lose its contribution when the scorer cannot see the relevant assertion.
Short cross-encoder views substantially reduce delivered coverage in the tested pipeline.
Packing policies redistribute support without identifying a uniformly best policy.
Additional scoring work does not change complete coverage in the tested refill comparisons.
We test generality by varying retrieval and workload conditions rather than assuming one cap order is universally preferable.
The 2048-token post-cap gain recurs with a second cross-encoder but is not established for every retriever.
Budget curves show how the available context changes coverage across document renderings.
The baseline comparison separates absolute coverage from the effect of moving an active cap.
Support structure changes the descriptive pattern of cap-order differences.
The paired URL intervention does not establish that higher source concentration uniformly amplifies the cap-order effect.
Source-policy enforcement addresses admissibility, a different question from retaining designated pages.
These comparisons support a conditional diagnosis of evidence loss rather than a universal configuration rule.
We evaluate generated answers separately because available support does not guarantee that the generator uses it correctly.
The original answer study uses a fixed generator and 512-token evidence across matched conditions and negative controls.
Pre-cap and post-cap have identical complete-answer outcomes at 512 tokens, while other configurations separate correctness from grounding.
The negative controls and citation protocol delimit what these answer scores establish.
A matched 2048-token follow-up directly tests the uncapped-versus-post-cap answer contrast.
Independent request measurements quantify the online work associated with evidence construction.
Pre-capping reduces measured request time relative to post-capping in the timed sample.
The reported timings exclude model loading and answer generation and therefore are not end-to-end service latencies.
The findings motivate evaluating delivered support alongside source retention rather than replacing all outcomes with one score.
The controlled workload establishes mechanisms under stated assumptions, not their prevalence in deployed systems.
The oncology workload provides an exploratory check of annotated support in real documents.
The selection pilot finds no demonstrated benefit from changing the development metric alone.
A useful diagnosis identifies the failed stage while keeping recommendations conditional on the measured endpoint.
RAG systems and component benchmarks study how retrieval and context-construction choices affect the pipeline.
Content and citation evaluations motivate measuring evidence support beyond source identity.
Controlled benchmarks complement end-to-end comparisons by exposing the conditions behind aggregate results.
A source can survive context construction while the complete support needed from it does not.
Reproducible analysis requires linking each reported result to its inputs, configuration, and delivered-evidence trace.
AI tools assisted with the manuscript and experimental workflow, with the authors responsible for verifying the resulting content and measurements.
